source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 41 'Turtle's Escape' (told by Henry Spence, Bog, Westmoreland)

summary.en: Caught for dinner, Turtle warns his cook that his fat will mash if the pot boils — so Anansi must lift him out at every bubble. A blow of the turtle's nose raises the water, Anansi sets him by the pan-side to cool, and the dinner slides back into the pond.
summary.zh: 龜被捕入鍋，先行告誡：水一沸，肥肉必爛，須隨時提起。龜以鼻息鼓水，蜘蛛人驚慌之下把他移到鍋邊『降溫』——晚餐便滑回了池塘。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Turtle fooled Anansi one day. Anansi went out and caught one turtle, quite glad of the turtle. When he got home, Turtle knew Anansi was going to eat him and said, 'Brar Anansi, you know me fat? When you put me on, as the water boils up you take me off, 'cause fat will mash.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 41 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: So when the water got warm, Turtle blew his nose to make the water boil up. Anansi got frightened, said the turtle would mash! So he laid him down at the pan-side to let the fat cool so he would not mash — and Turtle ran away into the pond. Anansi lost his dinner.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 41, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Fire Burns Out the Spider's House

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 42 'Fire and Anansi' (told by Henry Spence, Bog, Westmoreland)

summary.en: Fire, unable to walk, requires a road of dry bush laid to his host's door. Anansi's wife, the Ground Dove, warns against the visit — he will burn the house and everyone in it — but the spider lays the trash anyway, and Fire, arriving in a great jump, burns Anansi, his house and everything except his wife.
summary.zh: 火不能行走，須沿乾柴鋪路來訪。蜘蛛人之妻地面鴿力勸莫邀——他必焚屋焚人——蜘蛛人不聽，照舊鋪柴；火到門前猛然一躍，焚蜘蛛人、焚其屋、焚盡一切，唯獨留下他的妻子。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; fire-as-personage tale linking to fire clusters. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Fire were good friends. Anansi came and saw Fire and they had dinner; then he invited Fire to come and see him. Fire told him he could not walk — from his house, Fire said, his host must lay a path of dry bush, and he would walk on top of the dry bush.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 42 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Anansi was married to Ground Dove, who told him no: he must not invite Fire, who would burn his house and burn him out. Anansi would not hear what his wife said and laid the trash on. Fire burned from his house, and when he came near Anansi's house he made a big jump, burned Anansi, burned his house, burned everything but his wife. Fire fooled Anansi!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 42, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 43a 'Tailors and Fiddlers' (told by David Roach, Lacovia)

summary.en: At the ball the tailor Quit-quit's fiddle outdraws the spider's until Anansi's 'Me nyam-nyam taya' wins the girls. Quit-quit retorts that 'taya' is nothing; Anansi demands a suit of clothes that cannot be matched, and the tailor cuts it from maggot-flies — which, smelling the dinner meat at the ball's end, run off and leave the fiddler naked.
summary.zh: 舞會上裁縫的琴聲起初蓋過蜘蛛人，直到蜘蛛人奏出『我吃了肉泥』贏得姑娘們。布特布特反唇相譏；蜘蛛人便索要一套『無人能及』的衣裳，裁縫便以蛆蠅裁成——宴罷肉香一起，蛆蠅四散，琴師當眾裸身。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; fiddle-contest type. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Lizard went to a ball. Anansi was a fiddler, Lizard a tailor; Quit-quit was the fiddler's rival. Anansi played 'turn, turn, turn' and all the girls went round Brar Quit-quit; then Anansi played 'Me nyam-nyam taya!' — and it pleased the people, all the girls crowding round Brar Anansi. Brar Quit-quit said, 'Taya no somet'ing!' Anansi came in with his music — 'Me nyam de somet'ing! If taya no somet'ing, whe' are de somet'ing?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 43a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brar Anansi then said the tailor must make him a suit of clothes that could not be matched; Brar Quit-quit told him it must be made out of maggot-fly. After the ball they went to dinner — and when the maggot-flies smelled the meat, they ran off and left him naked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 43a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 44 'Spider Marries Monkey's Daughter' (told by May Ford, Newmarket)

summary.en: Monkey scorns Spider as too fast a suitor; Green-lizard's counter-plan is a guessing riddle — 'Miss Nennan-kennan-wid-a-turn-down-gown' — which only the spider, tipped off by the same lizard, can answer. Married with a baby in his arms, Anansi sings his own secret — 'A me cunnie mak me get yo' mama' — while the wife is at the pond; Monkey, arriving to hear it, grabs away the baby and kills Spider, and the baby drops dead from his hand. So never kill a spider: whatever you have in hand will surely break.
summary.zh: 猴嫌蜘蛛人太輕浮，綠蜥蜴獻策：以謎語婚試——『穿下垂裙的南南肯南小姐』——唯蜘蛛人得蜥蜴泄題而答中。婚後抱嬰獨守，蜘蛛人自鳴得意唱出機密：『全憑我機智娶到你媽』；猴子聞歌而至，奪嬰殺蛛，嬰兒亦墜地而死。故曰：莫殺蜘蛛——手中之物必隨之而碎。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; hidden-name riddle marriage links to Yoruba hidden-name traditions (cross-ref motif family).

passages.text: Bredder Monkey had a daughter whom Bredder Spider wanted to marry. Monkey did not want Spider to marry his daughter, thinking him too fast and beneath him — he only kept Spider company because he found him useful. He jumped to Bredder Green-lizard: 'Fancy! Bredder Spider want to marry me daughter! I don't want to hurt his feelings, as he is useful to us, so help me to get out of it.' Green-lizard answered, 'I tell you a way, man. Call her Miss Nennan-kennan-wid-a-turn-down-gown, and whoever guesses her name marries her — for Bredder Spider never can guess that!' Then the lizard went direct and told Bredder Spider the name to say.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 44 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Monkey sent out word to all the gentlemen who wanted to marry his daughter to come and guess her name. Not one could tell it until Bredder Spider came and said, 'Miss Nennen-kennan-wid-a-turn-down-gown.' So Bredder Spider got the daughter and married her. When his wife had a baby, she left the pickney with Spider and went to the pond; and Spider, thinking her gone, started to sing, 'Hush, me pickney, hush me baby — a me cunnie mak me get yo' mama!' His wife turned back — 'What is that you sing?' — and he answered only, 'Hush, me pickney! Hush, me baby! It's a good t'ing marry yo' mama?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 44, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bredder Monkey had been coming to see him and heard what Bredder Spider was singing. 'So that is how you got my daughter!' — and he grabbed away the baby and killed Spider. And as he killed Spider, the pickney dropped out of his hand dead. So never kill a spider, as whatever you have in hand will be sure to break.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 44, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 45 'The Chain of Victims' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Anansi borrows a dollar from Hog, Dog, Monkey, Tiger and Lion — each 'repayable tomorrow at twelve'. Next day the creditors arrive one by one, and the spider sends each successive guest into the back room with a warning to kill the one before: Hog kills nothing, Dog is sent after Hog, Monkey after Dog, Tiger after Monkey, and Lion finally kills Tiger. Anansi then calls Lion out to a deep hole by the kitchen 'to put on hot water', and the lion breaks his neck in it — leaving the spider alone with five creditors' bones to crack at night.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人向豬、狗、猴、虎、獅各借一元，約定『明日十二時來取』。翌日債主逐一登門，蜘蛛人卻把每位客人送進後屋，並囑其殺掉前一位；獅子終於殺了老虎。隨後蜘蛛人喚獅子到廚房邊深坑旁『燒熱水』——獅子墜坑折頸。蜘蛛人獨得五份『骨頭』，夜裡慢慢敲。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale (debt-chain / ogre-kill type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi saw Brar Hog and said, 'Brar Hog, lend me a dollar — tomorrow, twelve o'clock, come for it.' He saw Brar Dog and said the same; Brar Monkey, the same; Brar Tiger, the same; and Brar Lion, the same. Next day he heard a knock at the door — 'Me, Brar Hog' — and Hog came in and stayed talking until another knock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 45 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Me, Brar Dog.' Anansi told Brar Hog to run into that room, for Dog was too bad — if he caught him he would kill him. When Dog came in they talked until Monkey knocked, and Anansi sent Dog into the room, telling him that when he went in he would see Brar Hog under the bed — kill him. Monkey and Anansi talked until Tiger knocked: 'Brar Monkey, run into that room and hide, or Tiger catch you!' When Brar Tiger came in they talked until Lion knocked, and Anansi sent Tiger in with the same instruction about Monkey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 45, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: As Lion came in, Anansi told him: 'Look here! Plenty of meat. Brar Tiger gone in there; you are going to kill him!' Lion went in and killed Tiger. Meanwhile Anansi went out the kitchen door, dug a deep hole, and called, 'Brar Lion, run come here! We go put on little hot water to clean up those fellahs!' As Lion jumped out of the house, feeling so glad, and galloped to the kitchen, he got down into the hole and broke his neck. Anansi said, 'You brute! Look how much money I borrowed from you, and I have all your bones to crack tonight!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 45, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Tumble-bug Rolls in the Dung

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 46 'Why Tumble-bug Rolls in the Dung' (told by William Forbes, Dry River)

summary.en: The king offers his daughter to whoever brings a jar of money. Tumble-bug fills his jar with coin; Anansi fills his with cow- and horse-dung. At a wayside shop the two jars are swapped during a bread errand, and before the king Anansi's jar showers true silver while Tumble-bug's flings dung — 'Take it up, take it up, you nasty fellow, carry it out of the missis yard!' — which is why Tumble-bug rolls in filth to this day.
summary.zh: 國王懸賞：獻上一罐錢者可娶公主。推糞蟲罐中是錢，蜘蛛人罐中填牛馬之糞。途中兩罐在商店被調換；國王面前，蜘蛛人的罐子金幣嘩嘩傾瀉，推糞蟲的罐子滾出糞便——『撿起來！撿起來！你這骯髒的傢伙，把髒物帶出小姐的院子！』推糞蟲至今在穢物中打滾，便是由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a young lady, the king's daughter; her father said whoever came with a jar of money would get her to marry. Tumble-bug got a jar of money. Anansi got a jar and could get no money to put in it, so he got some cow dung and some horse dung and filled up the jar. As the two were going up to the young lady, they stopped at a shop, and the two jars favored one another. Anansi said, 'Brar Tumble-bug, let we go in the shop and get a drink' — and, sending him out for bread, took up Tumble-bug's jar and left his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 46 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Up in the king's yard Anansi said, 'Massa, must bring a clean sheet to throw the money out of the jar!' and he threw out money — wa-a-a-a-a! As Tumble-bug threw, he threw out horse-dung and cow-dung. Anansi said, 'Take it up, take it up, you nasty fellow, carry out the missis yard!' That is why you see Tumble-bug roll in filth until today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 46, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why John-crow Has a Bald Head

region.en: St. Ann's Bay and Bog, Jamaica

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 47 'Why John-crow Has a Bald Head' (a, Margaret Brown, St. Anne's Bay)

summary.en: Anansi, nursing his grudge against John-crow for stealing his nests, invites the crow alone to a wedding feast — then stages a 'baptism' that uses nothing but boiling water: every guest dips his head into the copper. The scalded crow, in the paired dance version, receives a ladle of hot pop flung on his head for dancing too neatly — and no John-crow in this world has had a feather on his head since.
summary.zh: 兀鷲屢偷蛛巢，蜘蛛人懷恨在心。他獨邀兀鷲赴婚宴，宴後舉行『洗禮』——洗禮用的除了滾水別無他物：每位客人把頭浸入大銅鍋。另一版本：兀鷲舞步太過出色，蜘蛛人以滾粥一瓢潑頂，把那顆頭上的羽毛燒個精光——從此世間兀鷲再無一羽覆頂。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. The 'baptism' frame is folk-comic use of a church term. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi always had a grudge against John-crow: whenever he made his nest, the Crow flew on it and caught it up, and he could never keep a nest. So he said he was going to marry, and he was going to invite no one but Crow; and he had a big dinner, and no one was at the table but Crow. After the eating and drinking were done, he said he was going to have a baptism — but he did not baptize with anything but boiling water. After the water boiled, he took it off, ordered Crow to sit round the copper, and dipped every one's head into the water — and that is why Crow has a bald head today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 47a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired telling, Anansi and John-crow had a ball one night, and dinner was found for all the dancers. John-crow was a great stepper and could step better than Anansi; finding John-crow danced neater than he, Anansi got vexed. After the dinner, when the pop was hot, he told John-crow he must dance up to the pop — and just to be rid of John-crow that night, he took a ladle and dashed the hot pop right up on his head, and all John-crow's head stripped off. All the John-crows in this world never have had a feather on their heads since: Anansi burned them off with hot pop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 47b 'The Dance' (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 48 'Why Dog Is Always Looking' (told by Moses Hendricks, Mandeville)

summary.en: Scouting land to rent, Anansi and Dog both fall for the same field. The spider boasts that his father once planted yams on that very spot — yams that bore 'big like me leg!' — and Dog, whose legs are worth more than thread, walks off to look round instead: which is why, when you are eating, a dog is sure to be looking at you.
summary.zh: 尋地租耕，蜘蛛人與狗同時相中一塊好地。蜘蛛人誇稱父親曾在彼處種薯，結的薯『大得像我這條腿』——而蜘蛛人的腿細如線。狗兒寧可去處處張望也不願與他合夥——所以如今你吃飯時，狗總在一旁盯著看。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Dog were friends. They wanted to go into cultivation, so both of them went out in search of good land to rent and came across a nice bit of land; Anansi fell in love with the spot, and Dog fell in love with the spot too. Anansi said to Dog he remembered when he was a little boy his father planted yams on that very spot — 'and the yams did bear.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 48 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Dog asked how big they bore. Anansi said, 'Brar Dog, they bear big — big like me leg!' (Anansi's leg is just like a thread.) Brar Dog said, 'Before I work and plant yam, and the yam not bigger than your leg, I sooner walk round and look!' That is the reason why, when you are eating, a dog is sure to be looking at you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 48, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Rocks at the River Are Covered with Moss

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 49 'Why Rocks at the River Are Covered with Moss' (told by Sarah Vassel, Bog, Westmoreland)

summary.en: Eating at the river-side, Anansi refuses a begging rock-stone a share of his meal — and when he tries to rise the stone holds him fast until a hidden passerby hauls him up, leaving half his skin on the stone: moss grows on the rocks at the river-side, and Anansi's skin grows there.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人在河邊進食，乞食的岩石討不到一口，便在他起身時死死攥住他；藏在林中窺伺的路人最後將他拔起——蜘蛛人半張皮留在了石上：河邊的石頭上長苔，那是蜘蛛人的皮。

sensitivity.note: Etiological landscape tale (origin of river-stone moss). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi was going out one day and stopped at the river-side eating. A rock-stone begged him, and he would not give it any. After he had eaten his fill and wanted to get up, the rock-stone held him and he could not get up — and began to bawl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 49 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: A man was coming past at the same time and asked, 'Bredder Anansi, who has been crying here?' Anansi said he did not know; the man went inside the bush and hid. Anansi hollered, and the man came out and caught him by his two hands and drew him right up — half of his skin left on the stone. Moss grows upon the rock-stones at the river-side: Anansi's skin grows there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 49, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924 print), tale 50 'Why Ground-dove Complains' (told by Simeon Falconer, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Tiger hires Dove to help watch his corn by night; Dove keeps the watch while Tiger sleeps — and by day destroys the corn himself. When Tiger, tipped to the scheme, dodges in the ground and catches the raiding gang, he slaps the traitor on the ears; the dove has been singing 'Me ears! me ears!' ever since.
summary.zh: 虎雇鴿子夜間守玉米；虎睡覺，鴿守夜——白天卻親自毀田。虎識破奸計，白日伏於地中擒獲劫掠的鴿群，摑其耳光；地面鴿自此哀唱『我的耳朵！我的耳朵！』至今。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Tiger was planting corn, and birds and everything were destroying the corn, so he got Dove to help him watch who was destroying it. After they sat up the whole night watching the corn, the next day Tiger went to sleep. Bredder Dove went back in the day and destroyed the corn himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 50 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: So the next day Tiger went in the day and dodged in the ground. Bredder Dove had a gang, and Tiger was slapping him on the ears as the gang was caught — and he sang out, 'Me ears! me ears! me ears!' And from that day to this the dove sings, 'Me ears!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 50, ending (2024); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 51 'Why Hog Is Always Grunting' (told by Norman Hilton, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: Bathing with Dog by the river-side, Hog takes off his mouth for the diving contest — and Dog, surfacing first, swims away with it. The mouthless hog surfaces grunting for his missing face, and has grunted ever since.
summary.zh: 豬與狗在河邊同浴，豬為比賽潛水卸下嘴巴；狗先冒頭，叼起豬嘴泅走。失去嘴的豬浮出水面，尋不著自己的嘴，只能哼哼作聲——豬的哼哼自那日起再未停過。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale (detachable-mouth motif). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Brar Hog and Brar Dog lived close by the river-side, and Brar Dog said to Brar Hog, 'Come! we get a bathe!' Brar Hog agreed, took off his mouth, and Brar Dog and Brar Hog jumped into the water. Brar Dog said, 'Come! let us see who can dive longer than the other.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 51 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two of them dived underneath the water. Brar Dog came up, jumped out of the water, took Brar Hog's mouth and went away with it. When Brar Hog came out of the water searching for his mouth and could not find it, he said, 'Humph! Brar Dog take a me mouth!' That is why Brar Hog is always grunting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 51, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Toad Croaks in the Wild Pine
title.zh: 蟾蜍何以在野松中呱呱

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 52 'Why Toad Croaks' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: The axe-magic bride contest — cut the cotton tree that fastens back its own chips — is won by Toad, who flings a pocketful of ashes at every flying chip until the tree falls. At the celebration 'washing', a great pot of boiling water is overturned over the stripped bridegroom-to-be, who jumps into the wild pine; every night to this day you hear him cry out, 'Kwoka soaka!'
summary.zh: 砍不斷自己復合的棉木樹——婚試之謎被蟾蜍破解：每有木屑飛回，他便撒一把懷中灰燼，砍倒大樹。慶功『淨身』時，一大鍋滾水被傾覆在剝光的準新郎身上；蟾蜍跳入野松，至今夜夜聽他哀叫『誇卡索卡！』

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale; axe-magic contest links to worldwide 'impossible task' cycle. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: One man had a daughter. He said, 'There is a cotton tree; the man who cuts down that cotton tree marries my daughter.' Every man went to cut it, and soon the cut chips fastened back, so they could not get the girl to marry. Toad said he would fell it. Toad filled his pocket with ashes, and every chop he chopped he flung the ashes upon the tree when the chips flew — and they could not fasten. So Toad did and did until he felled the cotton tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 52 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The master had a long barbecue and told him, 'Now you must go down there and strip yourself, and I will pour on the water to let you skin.' All this time a big pot of hot water was boiling on the fire; so they turned over the pot of hot water and said, 'Brar Toad, water come! Take your rubbing cloth.' And Toad jumped into the wild pine; up to this day, every night you hear him cry out, 'Kwoka soaka!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 52, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 53 'Why Woodpecker Bores Wood' (told by Samuel Wright, Maroon Town)

summary.en: A dying mother's wish to be buried in stone proves impossible: Woodpecker bores and bores and returns confessing failure, and lays her in wood instead — which is why the woodpecker bores the wood.
summary.zh: 垂死的母親願葬於石中；啄木鳥啄石不成，回來認罪，改葬母親於木中——啄木鳥啄木之習，便由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale with filial-piety frame. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a bird called Woodpecker who promised his mother to bury her in a stone, and went all about telling all his friends that he was going to bury his mother in a stone. The mother was poorly unto death, and he went to bore a stone — then turned back and said, 'Mother, I try the stone but I can't bore it. I'll bury you in a wood.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 53 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: And he bored the wood with his bill, working it wider and deeper day by day, until it was fit to receive her. After the death of his mother, he buried her in a wood, in the hole he had bored. That is the reason the woodpecker bores the wood, and bores it to this day, making the little round doors and windows of the dry trees for the dead of his kind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 53, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Crab Is Afraid after Dark

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 54 'Why Crab Is Afraid after Dark' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Promised a head by God tomorrow, Crab sings and dances his gratitude all night until he muddies the water; God refuses him the head — 'if you get a head you will do worse' — and decrees he shall carry his head on his shoulders all the days of his life, trusting no shadow after dark lest he be picked up and thrown into someone's basket.
summary.zh: 螃蟹得神應許明日賜頭，歡歌狂舞至攪渾河水；神怒而拒賜——『得了頭你會更壞』——並判他終生以肩負首，入夜後不敢信任何影子，唯恐被人拾起扔進籃中。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Crab went to God to give him a head. God told him he must go back: 'Tomorrow come, I will give you a head.' After Crab was going home he rejoiced in himself, singing, 'Tank God, tomorrow God a'mighty gi' me head! Tank God, tomorrow God a'mighty gi' me head!' He danced until he muddied the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 54 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day he went to God a'mighty to get his head. God told him, 'Stop! Before you have gotten a head, you go and muddy the water; then if you get a head you will do worse. So you must carry your head upon your shoulder all the days of your life.' So when Crab was returning home, when he got to Orange Bay and stood there, he would not trust a shadow after dark, for he does not know when they will pick him up and throw him into a basket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 54, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 55 'Why Mice Are No Bigger' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Robin Mice-rat wants to 'turn big man'. The Saviour sets him the test of killing his oldest uncle; the first night he only strikes him, and the blabbing uncle — boasting of the temple-blow that would have finished him — shows the very spot to the disguised nephew, who returns and kills him there. The Saviour refuses promotion: 'You little bit of man, go kill your oldest uncle, then if I let you turn bigger you will do worse!' — and mice stay small.
summary.zh: 老鼠羅賓想『變成大人』。救主設考：去殺大伯。第一夜他只是打了一下；大伯事後炫耀『幸而只中此處』，指點太陽穴位置——化裝歸來的姪兒依言補上一擊，將他打死。救主拒其升格：『你這點小人，殺了大伯還想變大？只會更壞！』——老鼠便再未長大。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale with violent folkloric content, recorded as folk narrative. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There is a man named Robin Mice-rat going to his uncle's house. He and the uncle stayed in the dark the whole time; when he was going away, he said good-by, took a stick and struck his uncle. At this time he went to our Saviour and said he wanted to turn big man; the Saviour told him that if he wanted to turn big man he must go and kill his oldest uncle. So, as the uncle never died, he went back the next night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 55 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Talking with his uncle, he heard the account: 'That fellow Robin came here last night; when he was going away, he took a stick and struck me on the head. But if he had caught me here (pointing to the temple), the fellow would have got me.' So as the uncle showed him the place, when he got up he met his uncle at the said place and killed him stiff dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 55, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day he went to his Saviour to be turned into a big man. The Saviour said to him, 'You little bit of man, go kill your oldest uncle — then if I let you turn bigger, you will do worse!' So from that day, that is the reason you see mice don't grow bigger, to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 55, ending (1924); not verbatim.
